beats.say: You thought the cavalry charge was the only surprise at Beersheba, but the water wells hid a deeper gamble.
At dawn on October 31, 1917, General Allenby ordered the 4th Light Horse to ride straight through the Ottoman defenses.
The secret? Engineers had secretly lowered the main well's draw-down, ensuring fresh water for the advancing troops.
While the world cheered the iconic leap, Ottoman commander Cevat Pasha scrambled to protect the wells, fearing desert thirst.
beats.visual: portrait of Cevat Pasha Ottoman commander

beats.say: His desperate counter-attack failed because the British had already wired a hidden pipeline from Gaza to the oasis.
beats.visual: map of secret pipeline Gaza to Beersheba

beats.say: The pipeline, built in secret by Australian sappers, delivered 12,000 gallons, turning the battlefield into a drinking-ground.
When the Light Horse surged, Ottoman soldiers slipped on the wet sand, their rifles clattering uselessly.
beats.visual: Light Horse charge on wet sand Beersheba

beats.say: By noon, the captured well fed 5,000 infantry, preventing a deadly dehydration retreat.
beats.visual: infantry drinking water at captured well Beersheba

beats.say: Historians now credit that hidden water supply as the true catalyst behind the swift victory.
The battle's legend lives on, but the wells' secret remains the unsung hero of Beersheba.
